Youth speaker Julian Grad argues that language didn't evolve so we could share our thoughts. Rather, we only began thinking clearly because we evolved language. In a talk spanning early humans around the fire, apples, lions and the birth of the inner "I", the Clifton College student explores how naming things builds the mind itself, why our deepest feelings escape words entirely, and how art steps in to say the unspeakable.

TEDxBristol 2025 was held at We The Curious (wethecurious.org), Bristol's much loved science centre on the city's historic harbourside, and beautifully filmed and edited by the team at Watch & Learn Productions (watchandlearnproductions.com).

This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organised by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx Julian came to TEDxBristol via the Bristol Education Partnership Youth Talks project. description:
When we think about accessible public transport, we usually picture ramps, wheelchair spaces and tactile signage. But what if the biggest barrier isn't the infrastructure at all?

Drawing on his lived experience as a blind traveller and his work as an engineer, inventor and founder of accessibility technology companies, Santiago Velasquez argues that truly accessible transport depends on something we've largely overlooked: the connection between travellers and drivers. By redesigning this critical part of the system, he shows how accessibility can become more reliable, more inclusive and more empowering for everyone.

Santiago reveals why accessibility isn't just about removing physical barriers — it's about designing systems that work for the people they're meant to serve. Santiago Velasquez is an electrical engineer and inventor whose work focuses on designing systems that make the world more accessible. title: The missing link in accessible transport | Santiago Velasquez | TEDxBrisbane

description: În discursul său, Renata Müler vorbește despre fragilitatea planurilor pe care ni le construim și despre ce se întâmplă atunci când viața ne obligă să le rescriem. Pornind de la experiența personală a diagnosticului grav primit de mama sa, Renata explorează adaptabilitatea, reziliența și tendința noastră de a eticheta anumite experiențe drept „cel mai rău lucru” care ni se putea întâmpla. Folosind metafora plantei Kalanchoe, ea arată că putem continua să creștem chiar și în condiții dificile, mai ales atunci când avem oamenii potriviți alături. Mesajul ei este o invitație de a nu trăi în grabă sau după planurile altora și de a ne aminti că avem libertatea de a ne rescrie drumul ori de câte ori viața ne schimbă direcția. Renata Müler are 26 de ani, șapte ani de studii universitare finalizate cu rezultate academice de excepție, două joburi și opt ani de implicare în voluntariat. Dincolo de performanțe, parcursul ei este definit de dorința de a-și construi propriul drum, fără a lăsa aște
title: Ars recreandi | Renata Müler | TEDxCopou Youth

We all grow up with timelines we’re told to follow, when to graduate, when to build a career, when to succeed, and where we’re supposed to be at each stage of life.

But what happens when your journey doesn’t follow that timeline?

In her inspiring TEDx talk, Nan Sandar Lin challenges the idea that there is one “right” timeline for everyone. She invites us to let go of comparison, embrace our own pace, and recognize that it’s never too late to rewrite the story we were given.

Because your timeline is yours to rewrite. After spending several years as a teacher, Nan Sandar made the unconventional decision to become a student again at the age of 21, returning to pursue IGCSE studies in support of long-term academic aspirations. This unique journey, from educator to learner, has provided firsthand insight into embracing change, navigating uncertainty, and redefining success beyond society's expected timelines.

author: TEDx Talks
description:
Stress isn't always panic, sometimes it's the quiet version: the textbook you read three times without absorbing a word, the six tasks that feel so heavy you end up scrolling instead, the "I'm fine" you offer when you're anything but fine. In this personal and often funny and sometimes emotional talk, Aaliya pulls apart what stress actually is and separates the things we genuinely need to worry about from the ones we only overthink.

Drawing on her own hardest year her grandmother's cancer diagnosis, the loss of her grandfather, and a university offer that came down to a single mark she shares how she moved from wallowing to action, one small step at a time. At the heart of the talk is a simple framework she leaned on again and again: Awareness to understand stress, Acceptance to face it, Action to move past it, and Resilience as what you become on the way back up.

It's an honest, hopeful reminder that the future feels less frightening when you stop living the pain before it arrives
title: Why Resilience Comes Before Recovery | Aaliya Chug | TEDxTSMS Noida Youth

description:
Once banned, buried, and abused by powerful institutions, psychedelics are back, and this time, they’re big business. In this talk, Dr. Brian Pace cuts through the hype of the so-called “Psychedelic Renaissance,” drawing on his experience as an educator and director at the watchdog organization Psymposia. Dr. Pace examines what medicalization and decriminalization promise and what they risk obscuring, ultimately begging the question: who benefits from the current psychedelic boom, and at what cost? 
 Dr. Brian Pace teaches in the Department of Plant Pathology. His research focuses on how psychedelic experiences interact with ideology and the socio-political context of the so-called psychedelic renaissance. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
title: Why Psychedelic Education Must Go Beyond Drugs | Brian Pace | TEDxOhioStateUniversity
